newsitem.title: USA: Intel countersues DEC, threatens to cut off Pentiums.
newsitem.headline: Intel countersues DEC, threatens to cut off Pentiums.

text.p: Intel Corp. fired back at Digital Equipment Corp. on Wednesday by suing the computer maker and threatening to cut off the supply of Intel Pentium chips, the critical components upon which Digital's $2.2 billion PC business is based.

As legal experts expected, Intel filed the lawsuit in response to a Digital Equipment complaint earlier this month alleging that Intel stole key technologies from Digital's Alpha chip and used it in its own Pentium.

But Intel escalated the battle beyond the courtroom by telling Digital executives in two letters that Digital does not have a long-term contract for Pentiums and that its most current purchase order runs out in the third quarter.
Intel spokesman Howard High would not say the letters were threats to cut off supply of Pentiums, but a "clarification" about where the companies stood with their purchasing agreements.

"Cutting off supplies is a riskier move for Intel, which I hope they've studied well," said Michael Barclay, an intellectual property lawyer with Wilson, Sansini in Silicon Valley. "I would be concerned about inciting counterclaims from Digital" alleging unfair business practices or violation of antitrust laws.

Digital began the high-stakes legal battle with its patent infringement lawsuit. Industry experts believe the company is making a giant gamble to rescue its floundering computer chip business in court -- even at the risk of cutting commercial ties to the world's largest chip company.

Digital is seeking unspecified damages that could cost billions of dollars. Attorneys following the case said the company likely will settle for some type of royalty agreement from Intel or favourable terms for purchases of PC components.

In its suit, filed in U.S. District Court in San Jose, Calif., Intel alleged breach of contract, claiming claimed that Digital refused to return confidential documents and product prototypes as Intel requested.

Intel lawyers also disclosed a letter, dated May 15, in which they told Digital executives that Intel is "not aware" of any long-term supply agreement for Pentium chips, as Digital had claimed when it filed the lawsuit. Digital's current purchase order "covers sales through (the third quarter)," the letter stated.
Intel's narrowly focused suit is a "smart move" because it quickly brings Digital to court on Intel's home turf, said trial attorney Kenneth Adamo with Jones, Day, Revis & Pogue.
But threatening to cut off supply of Pentiums could bring on anti-trust troubles for Intel, lawyers said.
In addition, Intel could spark resentment among PC makers by using its dominance of the microprocessor market to bully Digital, analysts said.
"This shows weakness on Intel's part," said Kimball Brown, chief PC analyst at market researcher Dataquest. "I don't know why else they are stooping to a move so low and stupid."
Digital said Wednesday that Intel's suit is a diversion and a "thinly veiled attempt to cause concern among Digital customers."
Digital, based in Maynard, Mass., also said it has a product agreement with Intel through 1999 and does not expect supply disruptions.
Shares of both companies fell. Intel lost $2.1875 to $165.125 in late Nasdaq trading, while Digital Equipment fell 87.5 cents to $36 in New York Stock Exchange trading.
